contract_plain_english: There is a single positive absolute constant c, fixed once and for all, such that: whenever X_1, ..., X_N are independent, mean-zero, sub-exponential random variables, then for every real t >= 0 the probability that the ABSOLUTE VALUE of the plain (unnormalized, unweighted) sum X_1 + ... + X_N is at least t is at most 2 exp( - c * min( t^2 / (||X_1||^2_{psi_1} + ... + ||X_N||^2_{psi_1}) , t / max_i ||X_i||_{psi_1} ) ), where ||X||_{psi_1} = inf{ t > 0 : E exp(|X|/t) <= 2 } is the sub-exponential norm. The crucial asymmetry is that the sub-gaussian branch divides t^2 by the SUM of squared norms while the sub-exponential branch divides t by the MAXIMUM norm. The prefactor 2 is explicit and comes from combining the upper and lower tails; c is an absolute constant with no numeric value and no dependence on N, on the X_i, or on t. The only hypotheses are independence, mean zero, and sub-exponentiality — no boundedness, no variance assumption — and the bound is asserted at t = 0 too.

source_evidence.observation: Rendered page reads: 'Let X_1, ..., X_N be independent, mean zero, sub-exponential random variables. Then, for every t >= 0, we have P{ |sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i| >= t } <= 2 exp[ - c min( t^2 / (sum_{i=1}^{N} ||X_i||^2_{psi_1}) , t / (max_i ||X_i||_{psi_1}) ) ], where c > 0 is an absolute constant.' The absolute-value bars around the sum are visible in the rendered page (pdftotext drops them).
'We are ready to state and prove a concentration inequality for sums of independent sub-exponential random variables.'

'Multiply both sides of the inequality S >= t by a parameter lambda, exponentiate, and then use Markov's inequality and independence. This leads to the bound (2.7), which is  P{S >= t} <= e^{-lambda t} prod_{i=1}^{N} E exp(lambda X_i).  (2.23)'  with S = sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i as introduced just above.

source_evidence.anchor: Proof of Theorem 2.8.1, display (2.24) and the surrounding sentences
source_evidence.observation: 'To bound the MGF of each term X_i, we use property e in Proposition 2.7.1. It says that if lambda is small enough so that  |lambda| <= c / (max_i ||X_i||_{psi_1}),  (2.24)  then E exp(lambda X_i) <= exp( C lambda^2 ||X_i||^2_{psi_1} ). Substituting this into (2.23), we obtain P{S >= t} <= exp( - lambda t + C lambda^2 sigma^2 ), where sigma^2 = sum_{i=1}^{N} ||X_i||^2_{psi_1}.' Note that here sigma^2 is a sum of SQUARED SUB-EXPONENTIAL NORMS, not a sum of variances.

source_evidence.anchor: Proof of Theorem 2.8.1, optimization step and footnote 8
source_evidence.observation: 'Now we minimize this expression in lambda subject to the constraint (2.24). The optimal choice is lambda = min( t/(2 C sigma^2) , c/(max_i ||X_i||_{psi_1}) ), for which we obtain P{S >= t} <= exp[ - min( t^2/(4 C sigma^2) , c t / (2 max_i ||X_i||_{psi_1}) ) ].' Footnote 8: 'Recall that by Proposition 2.7.1 and definition of the sub-exponential norm, property e holds for a value of K_5 that is within an absolute constant factor of ||X||_{psi_1}.'

source_evidence.anchor: Last paragraph of the proof of Theorem 2.8.1
source_evidence.observation: 'Repeating this argument for -X_i instead of X_i, we obtain the same bound for P{-S >= t}. A combination of these two bounds completes the proof.' — this is the origin of the two-sided event and the prefactor 2.
'The sub-exponential norm of X, denoted ||X||_{psi_1}, is defined to be the smallest K_3 in property 3. In other words, ||X||_{psi_1} = inf { t > 0 : E exp(|X|/t) <= 2 }.' (2.21)

source_evidence.anchor: Proposition 2.7.1 (Sub-exponential properties), statement and properties a-e with footnote 7
source_evidence.observation: 'Let X be a random variable. Then the following properties are equivalent; the parameters K_i > 0 appearing in these properties differ from each other by at most an absolute constant factor.' (a) P{|X| >= t} <= 2 exp(-t/K_1) for all t >= 0; (b) ||X||_{L^p} = (E|X|^p)^{1/p} <= K_2 p for all p >= 1; (c) E exp(lambda|X|) <= exp(K_3 lambda) for all lambda with 0 <= lambda <= 1/K_3; (d) E exp(|X|/K_4) <= 2. 'Moreover, if E X = 0 then properties a-d are also equivalent to the following one.' (e) E exp(lambda X) <= exp(K_5^2 lambda^2) for all lambda such that |lambda| <= 1/K_5. Footnote 7: 'There exists an absolute constant C such that property i implies property j with parameter K_j <= C K_i for any two properties i, j = 1, 2, 3, 4.'

binders: c: a positive absolute constant, existentially quantified OUTSIDE everything else — declared by the trailing clause 'where c > 0 is an absolute constant'
N: the number of summands, implicitly a positive integer (never explicitly bound)
X_1, ..., X_N: random variables on a common (unnamed) probability space
t: a real number, universally quantified by 'for every t >= 0'
conclusions: The event is TWO-SIDED: absolute value of the (unnormalized) sum, with non-strict inequality '>= t'

The first argument of the min normalizes t^2 by the SUM of squared sub-exponential norms; the second normalizes t by the MAXIMUM of the sub-exponential norms — the two normalizations are different quantities
The prefactor is exactly 2 and the constant c multiplies the whole min inside the exponent

In the PROOF, sigma^2 := sum_{i=1}^{N} ||X_i||^2_{psi_1} — a sum of squared sub-exponential norms, NOT a sum of variances (contrast with sigma^2 in Theorem 2.8.4)

Book convention: lower-case c and upper-case C denote positive ABSOLUTE constants with no numeric value and no dependence on N, the X_i, or t; the same letter may denote different constants in different places

Chernoff/Markov template (2.23) and the earlier bound (2.7) referenced from Section 2.2/2.3 (Theorems 2.2.2 and 2.3.1 are cited as the same pattern)
The two-sidedness and the prefactor 2 come from applying the one-sided argument to X_i and to -X_i and combining (printed page 37)

Interpretive remark (printed page 37): the bound is a mixture of a sub-gaussian tail for small deviations and a sub-exponential tail for large deviations, the latter produced by the single term with maximal sub-exponential norm, which alone has tail of magnitude exp(-c t / ||X_i||_{psi_1})
All random variables live on one common probability space; no measurability or integrability hypothesis is stated beyond mean zero and sub-exponentiality
